units.citation: Kimwanga et al. (2026). Who benefits from forest co-management? Heterogeneous welfare effects under rainfall shocks in Malawi. Trees, Forests and People.
units.quote:
Overall, VNRMC participation is 
associated with a 17.48% increase in forestry income and a 21.07 % in 
household non-forest income. Similarly, members of VNRMC have 3.2 
higher durable assets index and a 1.62% higher food consumption score 
than their counterparts non-participating members (Table 5).

relationship.outcome_raw: annual household NON-forestry income (agriculture, small business, other), VNRMC participants vs non-participants (pooled IPWRA ATT)

context.practice_as_described: household head is a member of a Village Natural Resource Management Committee (VNRMC) and engaged in forest co-management activities - 'a shared governance arrangement in which local communities and the state jointly manage forest resources'
context.note: Mechanism (p5): co-management 'grants communities' legal rights of access and sustainable use of forests, rights that can be translated into opportunities and income sources'; forest products act as a safety net during weather shocks. Forestry income = forestry wage labour, sales of wild fruits, mushrooms, insects, fauna, poles, timber, firewood. Cross-sectional survey of 743 households, 2023-2024 season; IPWRA ATT, PSM robustness. Reserves include two wildlife reserves (Majete, Vwaza Marsh). Table 5: ATT 0.191, significant at 5%. Authors do not give a pathway from co-management to non-forest income; heterogeneous by reserve (negative and significant at 10% in Chikangawa).
